sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Hypholoma fasciculare forms dense clusters of small to medium mushrooms. The smooth convex cap, about 2–7 cm across, is sulphur yellow with a darker yellow-orange to tan centre; fine veil fibres may remain at the edge. Crowded gills are attached to the stem: they start pale sulphur yellow, take on a distinctive green or olive cast, then darken to grey-brown or purplish brown as they mature. The slender yellow stem is often curved and browner towards the base. A temporary fibrous veil may leave a faint darkened zone, but there is no persistent membranous ring. The spore print is purplish brown. The flesh is yellowish and intensely bitter, but tasting a poisonous mushroom is not a safe identification method.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: A wood-decaying saprotroph, sulphur tuft grows in crowded tufts on stumps, fallen trunks, buried roots and other dead wood of broadleaf and conifer trees. It can appear to grow from soil where wood is buried. In Britain it may fruit over much of the year, with most records in summer and autumn; timing varies by region and weather.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: Hypholoma capnoides is similar on conifer wood, but its young gills are smoky grey rather than sulphur yellow to greenish. Brick tuft (H. lateritium) usually has a redder, brick-coloured cap and lacks the characteristic olive-green gills. The deadly funeral bell (Galerina marginata) and the edible sheathed woodtuft (Kuehneromyces mutabilis) may share woody habitats; both have brown rather than dark purplish-brown spore prints. Mixed clusters require examination of every mushroom, and a picture alone cannot establish edibility.

sections.title: Toxicity
sections.text: Sulphur tuft is poisonous and is classified by the German Mycological Society under the gastrointestinal syndrome. Reported illness can include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhoea, sometimes beginning around 5–10 hours after a meal. Severity varies and delayed symptoms also require prompt assessment because other wood-growing species, especially G. marginata, cause life-threatening poisoning. The historical report of a fatal case does not establish that sulphur tuft alone caused it. If ingestion is suspected, contact a poison centre or urgent medical service and retain any leftover mushrooms or meal for identification.

traits: Sulphur-yellow cap 2–7 cm wide, usually darker orange-tan at the centre
Crowded attached gills, yellow then greenish or olive, darkening with age
Slender curved yellow stem, browner below; fibrous veil, no lasting ring
Purplish-brown spore print; intensely bitter flesh, never test by tasting
Dense tufts on decaying broadleaf or conifer wood, including buried roots
safetyNote: Poisonous: may cause substantial nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, sometimes after a 5–10 hour delay. Do not eat or taste it. Suspected ingestion warrants prompt poison-centre or medical advice; a similar wood-growing mushroom may be the deadly Galerina marginata.
